doc.title: Peter Vacher interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001

title: The racial and political outlook of British jazz writers
summary: Leftward-leaning writers empathised with black Americans and treated jazz, blues and gospel as one black experience; Vacher preferred black players to Bix.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Is there an exotic factor to something, an art form that comes from another country?

I think all of us were kind of caught up in the racial element of it. You know a lot of the writers and a lot of the opinion formers were leftward leaning, right socialist people, and what they were empathizing with was of course the situation for black Americans, a tremendous interest in the blues, a tremendous interest in the formative experiences of black musicians, and of a sense of trying to do something to arrest or correct injustice. That was a powerful strand in the kind of reading I did and in the kind of opinion that was being promoted and published. So a tremendous interest therefore in that black manifestation. I mean when I was starting out, a jazz writer would be as keen to cover jazz in the conventional sense of improvised small group or big band music as he would blues or Gospel. That doesn’t apply today. But Max Jones would review and would enthuse about everyone from Marion Williams and the Stars of Faith, right through to Duke Ellington or Charlie Parker. They were all part of a piece as far as we were concerned. They were all aspects of the black experience, the black American experience. And in a sense they fit together as we saw it.
Did they have an interest in people like Frankie Trumbauer, Bix Beiderbecke?

Oh yes. Oh yes. Because the music of the white musicians that you’re mentioning there was actually released far more widely in Europe than was that of the black Americans perhaps. Those records were widely known. There is a whole sort of strand of people who are still very much devoted to that era of music or that particular genre of the music, oh yes. I wasn’t drawn to those. I was drawn to the black players. I was drawn, Bechet for sure, Kid Ory, and then fell heavenly for Jelly Roll, the Hot Fives, the Hot Sevens, you know, and worked my way through those great and triumphant series of recordings. You know they were like manna from heaven.
